name: Occam’s Razor
definition: Prefer the simplest explanation that adequately fits the data.
positive_example: Simplifying a differential diagnosis to the fewest likely causes improves speed and accuracy.
negative_example: Oversimplifying can miss rare but critical conditions.
crna_clinical_overlay: Favor the simplest explanation for hypotension (e.g., depth of anesthesia) before chasing rare causes, while staying vigilant for red flags.

name: Hanlon’s Razor
definition: Do not attribute to malice what can be explained by neglect or incompetence.
positive_example: Reduces conflict in team communication.
negative_example: Can excuse repeated unsafe behavior.
crna_clinical_overlay: Assume miscommunication before assuming intent when surgical flow breaks down.

name: Socratic Method
definition: Structured questioning to surface assumptions and refine thinking.
positive_example: Improves diagnostic clarity through targeted questioning.
negative_example: Time‑intensive in acute settings.
crna_clinical_overlay: Guided questioning during case review or M&M conferences.

name: Plato’s Cave
definition: Perceived reality may be incomplete or misleading.
positive_example: Encourages skepticism of first impressions.
negative_example: Excessive doubt can paralyze action.
crna_clinical_overlay: Monitors and vitals are representations, not reality — verify clinically.

name: Aristotle’s Golden Mean
definition: Optimal behavior lies between extremes.
positive_example: Balanced sedation avoids agitation or oversedation.
negative_example: False balance when extremes are not equivalent.
crna_clinical_overlay: “Stillness without oversedation” as an operational target. ---

name: Confirmation Bias
definition: Favoring information that confirms existing beliefs.
positive_example: Rapid pattern recognition in familiar cases.
negative_example: Missed diagnosis due to anchoring.
crna_clinical_overlay: Re‑evaluate assumptions when vitals diverge from expectations.

name: Cognitive Dissonance
definition: Discomfort from holding contradictory beliefs or behaviors.
positive_example: Drives learning and adaptation.
negative_example: Rationalizing unsafe practices.
crna_clinical_overlay: Recognizing discomfort when workflow efficiency conflicts with safety.

name: Dunning–Kruger Effect
definition: Low competence leads to overconfidence.
positive_example: Encourages humility in early learners.
negative_example: Overconfidence increases risk.
crna_clinical_overlay: Importance of graduated autonomy and supervision. ---

name: Opportunity Cost
definition: Value of the next best alternative forgone.
positive_example: Choosing case order to maximize throughput.
negative_example: Hidden costs overlooked.
crna_clinical_overlay: OR time spent troubleshooting is time not spent anesthetizing.

name: Diminishing Returns
definition: Increasing input yields progressively smaller gains.
positive_example: Prevents over‑engineering protocols.
negative_example: Premature optimization.
crna_clinical_overlay: Additional sedative beyond effect site benefit increases risk. ---

name: Feedback Loops
definition: Outputs feed back to influence future behavior.
positive_example: Continuous quality improvement.
negative_example: Reinforcing negative loops.
crna_clinical_overlay: Vital sign trends guiding titration.

name: Leverage Points
definition: Small interventions produce large system effects.
positive_example: Pre‑op communication reducing delays.
negative_example: Misplaced focus on low‑impact changes.
crna_clinical_overlay: Early IV placement improving entire day flow. ---

name: Risk–Reward Tradeoff
definition: Higher potential returns require higher risk.
positive_example: Informed investment strategy.
negative_example: Risk blindness.
crna_clinical_overlay: Balancing deeper sedation against airway risk. ---

name: Pareto Principle (80/20)
definition: Most effects come from a minority of causes.
positive_example: Focus on high‑impact workflow fixes.
negative_example: Ignoring edge cases.
crna_clinical_overlay: Identify the few causes of most delays. ---

name: Spaced Repetition
definition: Reviewing information at increasing intervals.
positive_example: Long‑term retention of protocols.
negative_example: Poor for time‑critical skills.
crna_clinical_overlay: Periodic review of crisis algorithms. --- # LLM Prompt Template — Dynamic Mental Model Selection ``` You are an expert reasoning assistant. name: Bayesian Updating (Bayes’ Rule)
definition: Update belief in a hypothesis as new evidence arrives (posterior ∝ prior × likelihood).
positive_example: Use new vitals/labs to re-weight differential diagnoses rather than “sticking” with the first guess.
negative_example: Bad priors or poor likelihood estimates can lead to confident wrongness.
crna_clinical_overlay: Treat changing EtCO₂, BP, SpO₂ as evidence that updates the most likely causes in real time.

name: Base Rates (Base Rate Neglect)
definition: Correct reasoning starts from prevalence/base rates before “special” evidence.
positive_example: Start with common causes of desaturation before rare syndromes.
negative_example: Ignoring base rates leads to over-diagnosing rare events.
crna_clinical_overlay: In ophthalmic MAC, airway obstruction/hypoventilation is typically more common than exotic etiologies.

name: Expected Value (EV)
definition: Choose actions by probability-weighted outcomes, not just the best-case.
positive_example: Picking a sedation strategy that lowers the expected airway intervention rate.
negative_example: EV can hide tail risks if consequences are catastrophic.
crna_clinical_overlay: Explicitly weigh “small chance, huge harm” events in airway planning.

name: Calibration
definition: Confidence should match accuracy over time.
positive_example: More reliable clinical judgment when you track predictions vs outcomes.
negative_example: Overconfidence fuels unsafe shortcuts.
crna_clinical_overlay: Track “I think this will be easy MAC” calls vs rescue/intervention frequency.

name: Regression to the Mean
definition: Extreme outcomes are often followed by more typical ones.
positive_example: Avoid overreacting to one unusually bad turnover day.
negative_example: Dismissing true system problems as “random variance.”
crna_clinical_overlay: Separate normal day-to-day variability from persistent bottlenecks.

name: Survivorship Bias
definition: Visible successes are overrepresented; failures are hidden.
positive_example: Don’t copy “fast MAC tricks” that worked only in cherry-picked cases.
negative_example: Overconfidence from only seeing the winners.
crna_clinical_overlay: Review near-misses and adverse events, not only smooth cases.

name: Goodhart’s Law
definition: When a measure becomes a target, it can stop being a good measure.
positive_example: Use throughput metrics with balancing measures (safety/quality) to prevent gaming.
negative_example: Chasing “turnover time” can increase safety risk.
crna_clinical_overlay: Pair flow KPIs with airway interventions, rescue rates, PACU LOS. ---

name: Theory of Constraints (TOC)
definition: System performance is limited by a primary bottleneck; improve it first.
positive_example: Fix pre-op readiness before optimizing intra-op micro-steps.
negative_example: Optimizing non-constraints wastes effort.
crna_clinical_overlay: Identify the daily constraint (pre-op, surgeon pace, PACU beds, transport).

name: Little’s Law
definition: Average WIP = arrival rate × time in system (L = λW).
positive_example: Reduce PACU time to reduce PACU crowding at the same arrival rate.
negative_example: Ignoring stationarity or mixing different patient classes.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use to reason about PACU capacity, intake, and discharge bottlenecks.

name: Parkinson’s Law
definition: Work expands to fill the time available.
positive_example: Time-box pre-op blocks to reduce drift.
negative_example: Over-tight time-boxing can create unsafe rushing.
crna_clinical_overlay: Set realistic but firm prep targets; build in safety buffers. ---

name: Swiss Cheese Model
definition: Accidents occur when multiple defense layers have aligned failures.
positive_example: Add redundancy (timeouts, checklists, alarms) to prevent single-point failure.
negative_example: Treating it as explanation without fixing systemic holes.
crna_clinical_overlay: Map latent failures (staffing, equipment, communication) plus active errors.

name: Normalization of Deviance
definition: Repeated rule-bending becomes “normal” if nothing bad happens—until it does.
positive_example: Early recognition prevents slow safety erosion.
negative_example: “We’ve always done it this way” becomes a hazard.
crna_clinical_overlay: Watch for creeping deviations in monitoring, sedation dosing, handoffs.

name: High Reliability Organization (HRO) Principles
definition: Mindful organizing in high-risk settings: preoccupation with failure, reluctance to simplify, sensitivity to operations, commitment to resilience, deference to expertise.
positive_example: Strong near-miss reporting culture.
negative_example: “Safety theater” without operational support.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use HRO principles to anchor safety while maintaining throughput.

name: Checklist Discipline
definition: Standardized check steps reduce omission errors.
positive_example: Prevents missed allergies, airway equipment checks, critical meds.
negative_example: Rote checkboxing can blind you to novel risks.
crna_clinical_overlay: Simple “MAC readiness” checklist (airway backup, suction, meds, monitors).

name: Signal vs Noise
definition: Separate meaningful change from random variation.
positive_example: Avoid titrating to artifact.
negative_example: Dismissing real deterioration as “noise.”
crna_clinical_overlay: Validate alarms (probe, cuff, waveform) before major interventions.

name: Situational Awareness
definition: Perceive, comprehend, and project what happens next.
positive_example: Anticipate OCR, movement, airway obstruction.
negative_example: Tunnel vision on one parameter.
crna_clinical_overlay: Maintain a “next 2 minutes” mental forecast during MAC. ---

name: OODA Loop
definition: Observe → Orient → Decide → Act; iterate with feedback.
positive_example: Faster detection and correction during instability.
negative_example: Cycling without re-orienting leads to repeated mistakes.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use OODA in airway/ventilation events: act quickly, then reassess.

name: PDCA / PDSA
definition: Plan → Do → Check/Study → Act for continuous improvement.
positive_example: Rapid-cycle testing of a new turnover checklist.
negative_example: “Plan-only” culture with no measurement.
crna_clinical_overlay: Micro-tests: pre-op call script, med prep layout, PACU handoff template. ---

name: Inversion
definition: Solve by asking how to fail and avoiding those paths.
positive_example: Identify how an airway event could happen and preempt it.
negative_example: Excessive risk avoidance blocks necessary action.
crna_clinical_overlay: “How do we lose the airway here?” → ensure backup and triggers.

name: Second-Order Thinking
definition: Consider downstream consequences (“and then what?”).
positive_example: A change that speeds turnover but increases PACU delays is a net loss.
negative_example: Analysis paralysis.
crna_clinical_overlay: Evaluate workflow changes across pre-op → intra-op → PACU, not locally. ---

name: BATNA
definition: Your best alternative if no agreement is reached; it defines walk-away power.
positive_example: Clear BATNA prevents accepting bad terms.
negative_example: Overstating BATNA can cause unnecessary impasse.
crna_clinical_overlay: Contract talks: define your outside option (other facility/locums/terms).

name: ZOPA
definition: The bargaining range where both parties’ acceptable terms overlap.
positive_example: Focus discussion on terms within the overlap.
negative_example: Negotiating when no overlap exists wastes time.
crna_clinical_overlay: Pay/coverage terms: identify overlap early to avoid endless rounds.

name: Anchoring
definition: Initial numbers/frames strongly influence final outcomes.
positive_example: Set a strong, defensible first anchor.
negative_example: Bad anchors distort internal judgment.
crna_clinical_overlay: First contract offer sets reference point—counter-anchor with standards. --- # CRNA / Clinical Systems Overlay — Extended Mapping | Clinical / Ops Context | Primary Models | Practical Use | |---|---|---| | Hypotension under MAC | Occam’s Razor; Bayesian Updating; Feedback Loops | Re-weight likely causes with each new data point | | OR Delays / Flow | TOC; Little’s Law; Pareto; PDCA | Find bottleneck, reduce time-in-system, iterate improvements | | Sedation Titration | Golden Mean; Risk–Reward; Signal vs Noise | Balance stillness vs airway risk; avoid titrating to artifact | | Safety Drift | Swiss Cheese; Normalization of Deviance; HRO | Detect weak signals, harden defenses, reinforce culture | | Crisis Response | OODA; Situational Awareness | Rapid cycle: act, reassess, adapt | | Contract Negotiation | BATNA; ZOPA; Anchoring; Second-Order Thinking | Define walk-away, find overlap, avoid downstream traps | --- # Expansion Pack v2 — Decision Biases, Risk, and Adversarial Thinking

name: Prospect Theory (Loss Aversion)
definition: People weigh losses more heavily than equivalent gains and evaluate outcomes relative to a reference point.
positive_example: Frame patient instructions around avoiding losses (missed drops → worse outcome) when appropriate.
negative_example: Loss framing can create fear-driven decisions.
crna_clinical_overlay: Expect stronger reactions to perceived losses (pain, delays) than equivalent gains (comfort, speed).

name: Framing Effect
definition: Choices change when equivalent information is presented as gains vs losses.
positive_example: Present options neutrally to reduce bias in consent discussions.
negative_example: Manipulative framing can steer choices unethically.
crna_clinical_overlay: How you present sedation options affects patient anxiety and cooperation.

name: Availability Heuristic
definition: People judge likelihood by how easily examples come to mind.
positive_example: Rapid recall helps detect common complications early.
negative_example: Recent rare events get overweighted and distort planning.
crna_clinical_overlay: Don’t let a recent “weird case” drive every plan—anchor to base rates.

name: Sunk Cost Fallacy
definition: Continuing a path because you’ve already invested time/money/effort.
positive_example: Recognize when to stop a failing process change and revert.
negative_example: Persisting with a bad plan increases harm.
crna_clinical_overlay: If a sedation strategy isn’t working, pivot early rather than “pushing through.” ---

name: Map–Territory Relation
definition: Models/representations are not reality; confusing them is a fallacy.
positive_example: Verify monitor readings with patient assessment.
negative_example: Treating dashboards as truth leads to blind spots.
crna_clinical_overlay: Waveforms and numbers are maps; the patient is the territory.

name: Falsifiability
definition: A claim is scientific if it can, in principle, be proven wrong by observation.
positive_example: Write protocols with measurable failure criteria.
negative_example: Unfalsifiable claims become dogma.
crna_clinical_overlay: Make hypotheses testable (e.g., “depth is the cause” → adjust and observe predicted changes).

name: First Principles Thinking
definition: Break problems down to fundamental truths and rebuild from there.
positive_example: Re-derive the “why” behind a policy to improve it.
negative_example: Overuse can ignore valuable heuristics.
crna_clinical_overlay: Rebuild sedation/airway planning from physiology + procedure constraints, not habit. ---

name: Premortem
definition: Assume the plan failed; generate plausible reasons in advance.
positive_example: Identify failure points before rollout.
negative_example: Can become pessimistic if not time-boxed.
crna_clinical_overlay: Before first case: “If we have an airway event today, what will have caused it?”

name: Signal Detection Theory
definition: Decisions balance hits vs false alarms under uncertainty; thresholds matter.
positive_example: Tune alarms/thresholds to reduce fatigue while catching true deterioration.
negative_example: Overly sensitive thresholds create noise; overly strict thresholds miss events.
crna_clinical_overlay: Manage alarm settings and personal thresholds for intervention.

name: Red Teaming
definition: Structured adversarial review to find weaknesses and failure paths.
positive_example: A colleague challenges assumptions in a new workflow.
negative_example: Turns combative without norms.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use “friendly red team” in protocol changes to catch safety regressions. ---

name: Incentive-Caused Bias
definition: Incentives shape perception and behavior, often distorting judgment.
positive_example: Align incentives with safety and quality, not just speed.
negative_example: Misaligned incentives drive gaming and corner-cutting.
crna_clinical_overlay: Throughput bonuses without balancing measures can erode safety culture.

name: Principal–Agent Problem
definition: Agents may act in their own interest rather than the principal’s.
positive_example: Clear contracts, transparency, and accountability reduce agency costs.
negative_example: Hidden information and weak monitoring worsen misalignment.
crna_clinical_overlay: Facility vs contractor incentives may diverge; design terms to align.

name: Moral Hazard
definition: Risk-taking increases when someone else bears the cost.
positive_example: Design policies so decision-makers share consequences.
negative_example: Encourages unsafe risk-taking.
crna_clinical_overlay: If the system absorbs downstream costs, upstream behavior may drift toward risk.

name: Prisoner’s Dilemma
definition: Individual rational choices can produce worse group outcomes than cooperation.
positive_example: Repeated cooperation improves long-run outcomes.
negative_example: One-shot thinking drives defection.
crna_clinical_overlay: Team trust reduces defensive behavior and improves flow + safety.

name: Nash Equilibrium
definition: No party can improve outcomes by unilaterally changing strategy given others’ strategies.
positive_example: Identify stable (even if bad) equilibria to know what must change.
negative_example: Stable doesn’t mean optimal.
crna_clinical_overlay: “Bad stable” contract dynamics persist until incentives/constraints change. --- # Expansion Pack v3 — Negotiation & Influence

name: Principled Negotiation (Interest-Based Negotiation)
definition: Separate people from the problem; focus on interests over positions; invent options for mutual gain; use objective criteria.
positive_example: Instead of arguing over a rate, jointly define coverage, call, overtime triggers, and quality expectations using market benchmarks.
negative_example: If one side negotiates in bad faith, “principled” framing can be exploited as delay.
crna_clinical_overlay: Contract talks: lock objective standards (market rates, coverage norms, liability allocation) and keep the relationship separate from terms.

name: Information Asymmetry
definition: One party has more/better information; outcomes depend on reducing or leveraging the gap.
positive_example: Request case mix, coverage logs, overtime history, and pay comparables to negotiate from facts.
negative_example: Over-sharing can weaken leverage; under-sharing can stall trust.
crna_clinical_overlay: Ask for OR metrics (late starts, add-ons, staffing) to support staffing/coverage language.

name: Signaling
definition: Actions that credibly communicate intent, quality, or constraints.
positive_example: Providing a clean counter-proposal with redlines and rationale signals professionalism and seriousness.
negative_example: Cheap signals (bluffs) erode credibility when challenged.
crna_clinical_overlay: Present a “ready-to-sign” version that signals you want agreement, not drama.

name: Credible Commitment
definition: Binding commitments change incentives and shape counterpart behavior.
positive_example: “We will cover X cases/week if A, B, C terms are met” creates clear decision structure.
negative_example: Over-committing reduces flexibility and increases downside.
crna_clinical_overlay: Commit to coverage only with guardrails (overtime pay, liability caps, termination symmetry).

name: MESO (Multiple Equivalent Simultaneous Offers)
definition: Present 2–3 packages that are all acceptable to you but different in structure.
positive_example: Offer three bundles (higher base/lower call; lower base/higher overtime; hybrid) to reveal preferences.
negative_example: If packages aren’t truly equivalent, you may anchor yourself into a worse deal.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use bundles to trade: scheduling flexibility, coverage load, pay terms, liability.

name: Logrolling (Trade Across Issues)
definition: Concede low-value items to gain high-value items; expand the pie.
positive_example: You concede a minor admin policy for stronger indemnity/insurance terms.
negative_example: Trading away “small” terms that later become big (e.g., vague duties).
crna_clinical_overlay: Treat indemnity, termination, pay, and control as “must-protect”; trade only truly low-risk items.

name: Anchoring & Bracketing
definition: Early numbers/frames shape the bargaining range; bracketing uses ranges to guide convergence.
positive_example: Counter-anchor with market data + a range tied to coverage and overtime assumptions.
negative_example: Accepting their anchor implicitly by negotiating only within it.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use anchors for both rate and liability caps; tie to objective benchmarks.

name: Reciprocity
definition: People tend to return favors/concessions; use strategically and ethically.
positive_example: Offer a small, visible concession to unlock a larger one.
negative_example: Conceding too early invites more demands.
crna_clinical_overlay: Offer operational wins (standardized handoff) in exchange for contractual protections.

name: Loss Aversion Framing (Negotiation)
definition: Counterparts are more motivated to avoid losses than to achieve gains.
positive_example: Frame contract changes as preventing staffing risk, surgeon disruption, and legal exposure.
negative_example: Overuse becomes fearmongering.
crna_clinical_overlay: “Without X protections, coverage stability is at risk” is often more persuasive than “we want more.”

name: Face-Saving
definition: Preserve counterpart dignity to enable agreement without humiliation.
positive_example: Provide objective criteria so they can justify concessions internally.
negative_example: Excessive face-saving can hide accountability for unsafe or unfair terms.
crna_clinical_overlay: Let admin “win” on optics while you win on substance (safety + liability + pay clarity).

name: BATNA Discipline
definition: Continuously improve and clarify your alternatives to avoid accepting bad deals.
positive_example: Active outreach to other centers strengthens your walk-away power.
negative_example: Imaginary BATNAs lead to miscalibration.
crna_clinical_overlay: Maintain realistic outside options (locums, other facilities, adjusted schedule).

name: Trust Equation
definition: Trust ≈ (credibility + reliability + intimacy) ÷ self-orientation.
positive_example: Consistent follow-through on coverage commitments increases negotiating power.
negative_example: High self-orientation (appearing purely self-interested) collapses trust.
crna_clinical_overlay: Pair hard boundaries with demonstrated reliability; reduces adversarial posture. --- # Expansion Pack v4 — Learning & Skill Acquisition

name: Deliberate Practice
definition: Targeted practice on weaknesses with clear goals, immediate feedback, and repetition.
positive_example: Rehearse airway maneuvers with feedback until error rates drop.
negative_example: Repeating what you’re already good at creates illusion of progress.
crna_clinical_overlay: Build micro-drills: jaw thrust positioning, nasal airway placement, mask seal, OCR response.

name: Retrieval Practice (Testing Effect)
definition: Actively recalling information strengthens memory more than re-reading.
positive_example: Quick “what’s the algorithm?” drills improve crisis recall.
negative_example: Poorly designed tests can reinforce wrong recall.
crna_clinical_overlay: Weekly 3-minute retrieval: airway rescue steps, hypotension sequence, local anesthetic toxicity response.

name: Interleaving
definition: Mixing related skills/problems improves discrimination and transfer.
positive_example: Practice different sedation scenarios back-to-back (OSA, anxious, COPD).
negative_example: Early performance feels worse and can demotivate.
crna_clinical_overlay: Alternate case types and complications in simulation to improve pattern recognition.

name: Desirable Difficulties
definition: Learning improves when practice is effortful in the right way (spacing, variability, retrieval).
positive_example: Simulated distractions to train attention control.
negative_example: Too difficult too soon causes failure and disengagement.
crna_clinical_overlay: Add controlled stressors (noise, time pressure) after baseline competence.

name: Cognitive Load Theory
definition: Working memory is limited; optimize instruction by reducing extraneous load and managing intrinsic load.
positive_example: Standardized cart layout reduces cognitive burden in emergencies.
negative_example: Over-simplifying removes necessary nuance.
crna_clinical_overlay: Standardize medication placement, labels, and setup to preserve bandwidth for vigilance.

name: Chunking
definition: Grouping information into meaningful units improves recall and execution.
positive_example: “Airway rescue chunk” vs memorizing isolated steps.
negative_example: Bad chunks encode wrong sequences.
crna_clinical_overlay: Chunk MAC workflow: monitor-check → positioning → sedation titration → rescue triggers → handoff.

name: Scaffolding
definition: Temporary supports enable performance beyond current ability; supports fade with competence.
positive_example: Stepwise independence in new techniques.
negative_example: Scaffolds kept too long create dependency.
crna_clinical_overlay: Graduated autonomy for new CRNAs: fixed protocols first, then adaptive decision-making.

name: Mastery Learning
definition: Progress is based on competence, not time; learners practice until a standard is met.
positive_example: Everyone reaches minimum airway rescue proficiency.
negative_example: Requires time and resources; can bottleneck training.
crna_clinical_overlay: Define mastery thresholds (e.g., successful mask ventilation under constraints) before unsupervised practice.

name: Feedback Quality
definition: Fast, specific, behavior-linked feedback accelerates learning; vague feedback does not.
positive_example: “Your chin lift angle is low—raise and rotate” improves next rep.
negative_example: Delayed or judgmental feedback reduces learning.
crna_clinical_overlay: Build short post-case feedback loops (what worked, what to adjust, one experiment next case).

name: Error Management Training
definition: Controlled errors + reflection improve robust performance and recovery skills.
positive_example: Simulate partial obstruction and practice recovery pathways.
negative_example: Uncontrolled errors in real cases create harm.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use simulation for error exposure; protect real patients with conservative thresholds.

name: Transfer-Appropriate Processing
definition: Learning transfers best when practice resembles real performance conditions.
positive_example: Practice crisis scripts aloud in the OR environment.
negative_example: Overfitting to one context reduces adaptability.
crna_clinical_overlay: Practice PACU handoffs using the actual template and constraints.

name: Dreyfus Model of Skill Acquisition
definition: Skill develops from novice → advanced beginner → competent → proficient → expert; rules give way to intuition.
positive_example: Sets correct expectations: novices need rules; experts integrate context.
negative_example: Mislabeling level leads to unsafe autonomy.
crna_clinical_overlay: Match supervision and case complexity to skill stage; avoid premature independence. --- # CRNA / Clinical Systems Overlay — Negotiation + Learning (Quick Map) | Context | Models | Practical Use | |---|---|---| | Admin contract negotiation | Principled Negotiation; BATNA; MESO; ZOPA; Anchoring | Convert conflict into packages + objective criteria; protect walk-away power | | Surgeon relationship + flow agreements | Face-Saving; Trust Equation; Logrolling | Preserve respect while trading across issues (timing, communication, readiness) | | New CRNA onboarding | Scaffolding; Cognitive Load; Mastery Learning | Standard work → progressive autonomy with competence thresholds | | Crisis readiness | Retrieval Practice; Chunking; Transfer-Appropriate Processing | Short drills in realistic context; strengthen recall under stress | | Skill development under time pressure | Deliberate Practice; Feedback Quality; Desirable Difficulties | Micro-drills + rapid feedback + controlled challenge | --- # Expansion Pack v5 — Difficult Conversations & Conflict

name: Difficult Conversations: 3 Conversations Model
definition: Every hard talk contains three parallel conversations: *What Happened* (stories, blame), *Feelings*, and *Identity* (what this means about me/us).
positive_example: Naming the identity threat (“I don’t want to be seen as unsafe”) reduces defensiveness and unlocks problem-solving.
negative_example: Ignoring feelings/identity causes repeated looping on facts without resolution.
crna_clinical_overlay: Post-event debriefs: separate factual timeline from emotions and identity (“I felt undermined / I felt unsafe”).

name: Nonviolent Communication (NVC)
definition: Speak in four parts: *Observation* (no judgment) → *Feeling* → *Need* → *Request*.
positive_example: “When turnover instructions change mid-case (observation), I feel rushed (feeling) because I need safety margin (need). Can we standardize a 2-minute heads-up? (request)”
negative_example: If used mechanically, it can sound scripted and provoke cynicism.
crna_clinical_overlay: Align safety + flow by translating frustration into actionable requests without blame.

name: “Make It Safe” (Psychological Safety Repair)
definition: When dialogue becomes unsafe, restore safety by *apologizing*, *contrasting* (what you don’t intend vs what you do intend), and *mutual purpose*.
positive_example: “I’m not accusing you of negligence; I’m trying to prevent repeated delays and keep patients safe.”
negative_example: Skipping safety repair turns “facts” into attacks.
crna_clinical_overlay: In a tense OR, briefly reset: shared goal = safe case + smooth flow.

name: Ladder of Inference
definition: People jump from data → meaning → assumptions → conclusions → beliefs → actions; conflict often comes from untested steps.
positive_example: “What did you see/hear that led you to that conclusion?” reduces story-driven blame.
negative_example: If used as “gotcha,” it escalates conflict.
crna_clinical_overlay: When someone says “anesthesia is slowing us down,” surface the data (what delays, when, why).

name: Steelmanning (Rapoport’s Rules)
definition: Before disagreeing, restate the other side’s view so they agree it’s accurate; then respond.
positive_example: Prevents strawman fights and builds trust.
negative_example: Time-consuming if done in high urgency moments.
crna_clinical_overlay: Contract talks: accurately restate admin’s constraints (budget, coverage) before asserting yours (liability, pay clarity). ---

name: SBI Feedback (Situation–Behavior–Impact)
definition: Feedback is most effective when it’s specific: *Situation* + *Behavior* + *Impact*.
positive_example: “In pre-op at 07:10 (S), you changed the plan without notifying anesthesia (B), which delayed start and increased patient anxiety (I).”
negative_example: Omitting impact makes it feel petty; omitting behavior turns it into character attack.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use SBI to address recurring workflow issues without blame.

name: Radical Candor
definition: High-performance feedback = *Care Personally* + *Challenge Directly*.
positive_example: Clear expectations reduce repeated friction.
negative_example: “Challenge without care” becomes aggression; “care without challenge” becomes avoidance.
crna_clinical_overlay: Address safety drift directly while preserving long-term working relationships.

name: Boundary Setting (Clear Yes / Clear No)
definition: Boundaries are explicit constraints on what you will/won’t do; ambiguity creates conflict.
positive_example: Prevents scope creep (“We do not provide free overtime coverage; here are triggers and rates.”)
negative_example: Vague boundaries invite repeated testing and resentment.
crna_clinical_overlay: Contracts and daily operations both benefit from explicit boundaries (coverage, breaks, rescue thresholds). ---

name: Thomas–Kilmann Conflict Modes
definition: Five default styles: competing, collaborating, compromising, avoiding, accommodating; choose based on stakes and relationship.
positive_example: Collaborate on safety-critical issues; compromise on low-stakes preferences.
negative_example: Defaulting to avoidance lets problems harden into culture.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use “competing” for immediate safety; “collaborating” for process redesign.

name: Fundamental Attribution Error
definition: Over-attributing others’ behavior to character and under-attributing to context.
positive_example: Reduces moralizing and improves system fixes.
negative_example: Over-correcting can excuse accountability.
crna_clinical_overlay: Before blaming a person for delays, check staffing, room readiness, and process design. --- # Expansion Pack v6 — Advanced Learning: Memory, Attention, Habit

name: Forgetting Curve
definition: Memory decays rapidly without review; timely refreshes prevent steep loss.
positive_example: Schedule brief refreshers after initial learning to preserve protocols.
negative_example: Assuming “once learned = permanent” leads to skill decay.
crna_clinical_overlay: Refresh rarely used crisis steps (e.g., LAST) on a cadence, not only annually.

name: Interference (Proactive / Retroactive)
definition: Old learning disrupts new (proactive) and new disrupts old (retroactive).
positive_example: Separate similar protocols during early acquisition.
negative_example: Mixing similar drug concentrations without strong cues increases error risk.
crna_clinical_overlay: Standardize concentrations/labels to reduce interference-driven medication errors.

name: Context-Dependent Memory
definition: Recall improves when learning and performance contexts match.
positive_example: Practicing handoffs in the actual PACU improves reliability.
negative_example: Overfitting to one environment reduces flexibility.
crna_clinical_overlay: Drill crisis scripts in-room with the same cart layout and language.

name: Sleep-Dependent Consolidation
definition: Sleep stabilizes and integrates learning; deprivation degrades performance and memory.
positive_example: Better retention and fewer errors after adequate sleep.
negative_example: Chronic sleep debt raises risk and slows learning.
crna_clinical_overlay: Recognize fatigue as a safety variable; protect sleep when possible before heavy days. ---

name: Attention Residue
definition: Task switching leaves residual attention on the previous task, reducing performance.
positive_example: Batch charting and messages reduces cognitive fragmentation.
negative_example: Constant interruptions degrade vigilance.
crna_clinical_overlay: Protect “vigilance windows” during induction/emergence and high-risk moments.

name: Vigilance Decrement
definition: Sustained attention declines over time, especially in low-stimulation environments.
positive_example: Micro-check routines and cues maintain attention.
negative_example: Long “quiet” cases can hide slow deterioration.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use periodic scan patterns (airway → ventilation → circulation → depth → field) to counter decrement.

name: Implementation Intentions (If–Then Planning)
definition: Pre-commit: “If X happens, then I will do Y,” increasing follow-through.
positive_example: “If SpO₂ drops below 92, then I reposition, open airway, increase O₂, and reassess within 30 seconds.”
negative_example: Poor triggers or rigid rules can reduce flexibility.
crna_clinical_overlay: Turn rescue thresholds into if–then rules to reduce delay under stress. ---

name: Habit Loop (Cue–Routine–Reward)
definition: Habits form via a trigger cue, a routine behavior, and a reinforcing reward.
positive_example: Make “pre-case checklist” automatic with a consistent cue (room entry) and reward (fewer surprises).
negative_example: Bad cues and rewards reinforce unsafe shortcuts.
crna_clinical_overlay: Design cues for safety-critical routines (suction check, backup airway ready).

name: Identity-Based Habits
definition: Sustained change sticks when tied to identity (“I am the kind of person who…”).
positive_example: “I’m a vigilant anesthetist” supports consistent monitoring routines.
negative_example: Rigid identity can block updating practices.
crna_clinical_overlay: Anchor team identity around “safe + smooth” to align daily behavior.

name: Environment Design (Choice Architecture)
definition: Change behavior by shaping defaults and friction in the environment.
positive_example: Standardized cart layout makes correct action easy.
negative_example: Poor design embeds errors into routine.
crna_clinical_overlay: Place rescue tools/meds in consistent locations; reduce reach and search under stress.

name: Variable Reinforcement
definition: Inconsistent rewards can strongly reinforce behaviors (good or bad).
positive_example: Use intermittent recognition to reinforce desired behaviors.
negative_example: Random “getting away with shortcuts” reinforces deviance.
crna_clinical_overlay: Catch and correct “shortcut rewards” before they become culture. --- # CRNA / Clinical Systems Overlay — Conflict + Learning (Quick Map) | Context | Models | Practical Use | |---|---|---| | Post-event conflict | 3 Conversations; Ladder of Inference; Make It Safe | Separate facts/feelings/identity; test assumptions; restore safety | | Performance feedback | SBI; Radical Candor | Specific behavior-level feedback without character attacks | | Interruptions during high-risk moments | Attention Residue; Vigilance Decrement | Protect vigilance windows; use scan patterns | | Protocol retention | Forgetting Curve; Retrieval Practice | Short recurring refreshers prevent decay | | Medication safety | Interference; Environment Design | Standardize concentrations/labels/layout to reduce confusion | | Behavior change | Implementation Intentions; Habit Loop; Identity Habits | Convert intentions into triggers and automatic routines | --- # Expansion Pack v7 — Influence & Persuasion

name: Social Proof
definition: People infer the correct action by observing what similar others do.
positive_example: Adoption rises when you show that “most teams already use the new handoff template.”
negative_example: “Everyone does it” can normalize unsafe shortcuts.
crna_clinical_overlay: Reinforce safety norms with visible compliance (timeouts, checklist use) so the default becomes “safe and consistent.”

name: Authority
definition: People comply more when guidance comes from recognized expertise or legitimate authority.
positive_example: Using evidence-based guidelines and medical director endorsement speeds protocol adoption.
negative_example: Blind obedience suppresses speaking up and creates safety risk.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use “deference to expertise” (not title) in the moment: whoever sees the risk leads the fix.

name: Liking
definition: People are more persuadable by those they like and feel connected to.
positive_example: Consistent warmth + competence reduces friction when you need to enforce boundaries.
negative_example: Over-indexing on being liked leads to weak boundaries.
crna_clinical_overlay: Build rapport early in the day so safety corrections land as teamwork, not criticism.

name: Consistency / Commitment
definition: People tend to align future behavior with prior commitments and identity.
positive_example: “Can we agree the priority is safe start times with no rushed induction?” creates a commitment you can reference later.
negative_example: Locking into a wrong commitment increases stubbornness.
crna_clinical_overlay: Get micro-commitments on safety steps (heads-up before draping, pause before incision) to reduce mid-case surprises.

name: Scarcity
definition: Perceived scarcity increases value and urgency.
positive_example: “We have a limited window to avoid cancellations if we don’t fix pre-op readiness.”
negative_example: Artificial scarcity becomes manipulation and erodes trust.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use real scarcity (PACU capacity, surgeon time, staffing) to justify process changes without drama.

name: Unity
definition: Shared identity (“we”) amplifies influence beyond simple liking.
positive_example: “We’re the team that runs safe and smooth” improves follow-through.
negative_example: In-group thinking can dismiss outsider warnings.
crna_clinical_overlay: Build a shared “safe + smooth” identity that supports both vigilance and throughput. ---

name: Contrast Principle
definition: Judgments shift depending on what is compared immediately before.
positive_example: Present the “worst acceptable” alternative first so the reasonable offer feels easier to accept.
negative_example: Manipulative contrasts trigger distrust.
crna_clinical_overlay: Show the difference between “uncapped indemnity + vague duties” vs “balanced terms” to clarify stakes.

name: Foot-in-the-Door
definition: Small initial compliance increases likelihood of later larger compliance.
positive_example: Start with a small process change (one standardized handoff line) before a full template.
negative_example: Can be perceived as sneaky if escalated too quickly.
crna_clinical_overlay: Pilot one room/day with a micro-protocol, then scale.

name: Door-in-the-Face
definition: A large request followed by a smaller request makes the smaller one feel like a concession.
positive_example: Ask for a robust package, then offer a smaller acceptable version.
negative_example: If the large ask is absurd, credibility drops.
crna_clinical_overlay: Present an ideal contract package, then a realistic fall-back package (both safe) to enable agreement.

name: Tactical Empathy (Labeling)
definition: Naming emotions (“It seems like…”) reduces threat and increases cooperation.
positive_example: “It sounds like you’re worried about budget predictability.”
negative_example: Fake empathy is immediately detected.
crna_clinical_overlay: In admin talks, label concerns first, then pivot to objective criteria and packages.

name: Mirroring
definition: Repeating the last 1–3 key words prompts elaboration and builds rapport.
positive_example: “Budget unpredictability?” → they reveal constraints you can solve.
negative_example: Overuse feels gimmicky.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use sparingly with surgeons/admin to extract the real blocker behind a complaint.

name: Motivational Interviewing (MI)
definition: Elicit change by exploring ambivalence; amplify intrinsic motivation (OARS: open questions, affirmations, reflections, summaries).
positive_example: Patients more likely to follow pre-op instructions when they generate their own reasons.
negative_example: If used to “steer,” it undermines autonomy.
crna_clinical_overlay: Pre-op anxiety: use reflective listening to reduce resistance and improve cooperation. --- # Expansion Pack v8 — Rapid Learning on Busy Clinical Days

name: Generation Effect
definition: Information you generate yourself is remembered better than information you only read.
positive_example: Write your own 5-step airway rescue sequence from memory.
negative_example: Generating wrong info can strengthen wrong recall.
crna_clinical_overlay: After a case, generate the “what I’d do next time” plan before reviewing notes.

name: Elaboration (Elaborative Encoding)
definition: Memory improves when you connect new info to existing knowledge (why/how links).
positive_example: Linking sedation dosing decisions to physiology improves transfer.
negative_example: Over-elaboration wastes time if not constrained.
crna_clinical_overlay: One-sentence “because” rule per lesson: “I do X because Y physiology.”

name: Elaborative Interrogation
definition: Ask “Why is this true?” to deepen understanding.
positive_example: Improves concept mastery with minimal extra time.
negative_example: Endless “why” can become rumination.
crna_clinical_overlay: “Why does EtCO₂ rise here?” → connect to hypoventilation/CO₂ load.

name: Self-Explanation
definition: Explaining steps to yourself improves learning and error detection.
positive_example: Catches gaps before they become errors.
negative_example: Over-talking can distract during high workload.
crna_clinical_overlay: Quiet self-explanation during setup (not during critical moments) improves reliability.

name: Feynman Technique
definition: If you can’t explain it simply, you don’t understand it; refine until simple.
positive_example: Forces removal of jargon and reveals missing steps.
negative_example: Oversimplification can omit edge-case nuance.
crna_clinical_overlay: Explain OCR management in plain language to a trainee; update your own understanding.

name: Method of Loci
definition: Use spatial memory (a “memory palace”) to store ordered items.
positive_example: Strong for ordered crisis algorithms.
negative_example: Setup time; may not fit all learners.
crna_clinical_overlay: Map crisis steps onto a familiar OR walk-through (door → cart → monitor → airway). ---

name: Microlearning
definition: Learning in small, focused units that fit into real constraints.
positive_example: 2-minute daily drills outperform monthly long sessions.
negative_example: Fragmented micro-lessons without structure become noise.
crna_clinical_overlay: “Two-minute protocol refresh” between cases (one topic only).

name: Just-in-Time Learning
definition: Acquire knowledge immediately before use; high relevance improves retention.
positive_example: Quick review of OCR triggers before a high-risk case.
negative_example: Over-reliance can reduce deep mastery.
crna_clinical_overlay: Pre-brief: 1 minute on the likely complication and your response.

name: Cognitive Offloading
definition: Reduce working-memory burden by storing steps externally (checklists, templates, cues).
positive_example: Improves performance under stress.
negative_example: Overdependence can reduce adaptability if aids fail.
crna_clinical_overlay: Pocket card for rescue thresholds + dosing guardrails.

name: External Cues (Context Triggers)
definition: Reliable cues prompt the right action at the right time.
positive_example: A visual cue on the cart prompts suction check every case.
negative_example: Too many cues create banner blindness.
crna_clinical_overlay: Minimal set of high-value cues only (airway backup, suction, vasoactive ready).

name: Spaced Retrieval (Rapid Variant)
definition: Very short retrieval sessions spaced across days beat long single reviews.
positive_example: Improves automatic recall of crisis steps.
negative_example: If you skip sessions, decay returns quickly.
crna_clinical_overlay: 30-second retrieval after lunch + end of day (same prompt), then once weekly.

name: Interruption Budgeting
definition: Treat interruptions as a scarce resource; protect high-risk windows.
positive_example: Fewer missed changes in ventilation or depth.
negative_example: Over-restriction can reduce team communication.
crna_clinical_overlay: “No non-urgent interruptions” during induction/emergence and instability. --- # CRNA / Clinical Systems Overlay — Influence + Rapid Learning (Quick Map) | Context | Models | Practical Use | |---|---|---| | Protocol adoption | Social Proof; Authority; Foot-in-the-Door | Make safe behavior visible; start with small pilots; get expert endorsement | | Negotiation dynamics | Contrast; Anchoring; Tactical Empathy; Mirroring | Reveal constraints; reframe terms; drive to packages and objective criteria | | Patient cooperation | MI; Liking; Framing | Reduce resistance; improve pre-op compliance and calm | | On-shift learning | Microlearning; Just-in-Time; Spaced Retrieval | Short drills between cases; pre-brief likely complication | | Vigilance protection | Cognitive Offloading; Interruption Budgeting | Externalize steps; protect high-risk attention windows | --- # Expansion Pack v9 — Persuasion Ethics & Anti-Manipulation Safeguards

name: Consent-Based Influence
definition: Influence is ethical when the other party retains meaningful choice, clarity, and the ability to decline without penalty.
positive_example: “Here are two options; either is acceptable. Which fits you best?” preserves autonomy.
negative_example: “Fake choice” framing (only one acceptable option) erodes trust.
crna_clinical_overlay: Pre-op discussions: ensure the patient understands options and can refuse without shame.

name: Transparency Principle
definition: Disclose intent and constraints; hide nothing material that would change a reasonable person’s decision.
positive_example: “My goal is to protect patient safety and stable coverage; here are the constraints we’re operating under.”
negative_example: Withholding material constraints becomes manipulation.
crna_clinical_overlay: Contract/process changes: explicitly state safety goals and trade-offs.

name: Reversibility (Golden Rule Test)
definition: If the roles were reversed, would you consider this influence fair?
positive_example: You’d accept the same framing if you were the counterpart.
negative_example: If it would feel coercive when reversed, it’s likely unethical.
crna_clinical_overlay: Avoid “pressure scripts” with anxious patients; use supportive clarity.

name: Proportionality
definition: The strength of influence should match the stakes and urgency.
positive_example: Stronger persuasion is justified for imminent safety threats.
negative_example: Using high-pressure tactics for low-stakes preferences is abuse.
crna_clinical_overlay: “Stop the line” is appropriate for safety; not for convenience.

name: Least Manipulative Alternative (LMA)
definition: Use the least manipulative technique that still achieves the necessary outcome.
positive_example: Start with clear facts + neutral framing before using any emotional leverage.
negative_example: Jumping straight to fear/urgency escalates distrust.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use objective data first (delays, safety metrics); escalate only if needed. ---

name: Red Flags for Manipulation
definition: Common markers: time pressure without cause, information withholding, shame/guilt leverage, moving goalposts, false dichotomies, inconsistent standards.
positive_example: Naming the tactic (“I need the data before deciding”) resets the frame.
negative_example: Seeing manipulation everywhere creates paranoia and blocks collaboration.
crna_clinical_overlay: Contract talks: watch for “sign now,” vague duties, asymmetric termination, and uncapped indemnity as coercive structure.

name: Precommitment to Decision Criteria
definition: Define your acceptance criteria before negotiating to avoid being pushed off-center by tactics.
positive_example: “We sign only if liability is capped, pay triggers are explicit, and termination is symmetric.”
negative_example: Criteria too rigid can miss creative packages.
crna_clinical_overlay: Create “minimum safe terms” and don’t renegotiate them mid-conversation.

name: Two-Key Rule (Independent Verification)
definition: Require two independent signals before acting on high-impact claims.
positive_example: Verify “policy requires this” with written policy + a second stakeholder.
negative_example: Over-verification slows urgent action.
crna_clinical_overlay: For major operational changes, require documented policy + leadership confirmation.

name: Slow Yes / Fast No
definition: Resist pressured agreement; decline quickly when core criteria are violated.
positive_example: Prevents regretful commitments.
negative_example: Overuse can appear uncooperative.
crna_clinical_overlay: “We can’t accept uncapped liability” is a fast no; package discussion is slow yes. --- # Expansion Pack v10 — Attention Under Stress & Error-Proofing

name: Yerkes–Dodson Law
definition: Performance increases with arousal up to an optimal point, then declines.
positive_example: Mild urgency sharpens vigilance.
negative_example: Excess stress causes tunnel vision and errors.
crna_clinical_overlay: Reduce unnecessary stressors during induction/emergence; keep arousal optimal.

name: Tunnel Vision / Attentional Narrowing
definition: Under stress, attention narrows; salient cues dominate and other cues are missed.
positive_example: Focus on airway during crisis can be lifesaving.
negative_example: Missed hypotension, IV infiltration, or surgical stimulus changes.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use a forced scan after the first intervention to re-broaden attention.

name: Startle Effect
definition: Sudden unexpected events degrade cognitive processing and motor performance.
positive_example: Training reduces startle penalties.
negative_example: Startle can cause freezing or impulsive actions.
crna_clinical_overlay: Simulate sudden OCR/brady events to reduce startle and improve response.

name: Cognitive Tunneling (Automation / Monitor Fixation)
definition: Over-fixating on one channel (monitor/alert) while missing broader context.
positive_example: Attention to a critical trend catches early deterioration.
negative_example: Ignoring patient/surgical field leads to late recognition.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use “patient-first check” whenever an alarm fires. ---

name: Poka‑Yoke (Mistake-Proofing)
definition: Design the system so errors are hard to make and easy to detect.
positive_example: Color-coded labels and standardized concentrations reduce med errors.
negative_example: Over-complex safeguards create workarounds.
crna_clinical_overlay: Standardize syringe labels, drawer layout, and concentration defaults.

name: Check–Challenge–Confirm
definition: Verify a critical item, challenge discrepancies, and confirm resolution.
positive_example: Prevents silent error propagation.
negative_example: Overuse for trivial items slows flow.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use for allergies, laterality, critical meds, and airway backup readiness.

name: “Sterile Cockpit” Rule
definition: During high-risk phases, minimize nonessential conversation and interruptions.
positive_example: Reduces missed cues during critical moments.
negative_example: If applied rigidly, can suppress essential communication.
crna_clinical_overlay: Induction/emergence/instability = sterile cockpit; routine maintenance = normal comms.

name: Standard Work + Deviations Log
definition: Define the best-known method; log deviations to learn and improve.
positive_example: Improves reliability and reduces variability.
negative_example: Over-standardization blocks needed adaptation.
crna_clinical_overlay: Standard MAC setup; log deviations (why, outcome) for iterative improvement.

name: Forced Functions (Hard Stops)
definition: Design constraints that prevent action until a critical step is completed.
positive_example: Prevents skipping key safety steps.
negative_example: Poorly placed hard stops cause workarounds.
crna_clinical_overlay: “No incision before timeout complete” is a justified forced function. --- # CRNA / Clinical Systems Overlay — Ethics + Stress + Error-Proofing (Quick Map) | Context | Models | Practical Use | |---|---|---| | Ethical influence with patients | Consent-Based Influence; Transparency; Reversibility | Preserve autonomy; disclose intent; avoid coercion | | Detecting admin manipulation | Red Flags; Precommitment Criteria; Slow Yes/Fast No | Avoid pressured agreement; hold minimum safe terms | | Managing stress performance | Yerkes–Dodson; Startle Effect | Keep arousal optimal; train for surprise | | Preventing fixation errors | Tunnel Vision; Cognitive Tunneling | Forced scan + patient-first checks | | Hardening systems | Poka‑Yoke; Check–Challenge–Confirm; Sterile Cockpit | Reduce error likelihood during critical windows | --- # Expansion Pack v11 — Error Taxonomy & Mitigations

name: Slips
definition: Correct intention, wrong action (often attention capture, distraction, or habit misfire).
positive_example: Recognizing a slip prompts environment fixes (labels, layout) rather than blame.
negative_example: Treating slips as “carelessness” prevents system learning.
crna_clinical_overlay: Wrong syringe grab due to look-alike labels → fix with poka-yoke, layout, labeling.

name: Lapses
definition: Memory failure (forgetting a step) despite correct plan.
positive_example: Checklists and cues prevent omission.
negative_example: Punishing lapses discourages reporting.
crna_clinical_overlay: Missed suction check → create cue at room entry + checklist discipline.

name: Mistakes (Rule-Based / Knowledge-Based)
definition: Wrong plan or wrong rule applied; action matches intention but intention is flawed.
positive_example: Drives training and decision support improvements.
negative_example: If treated as incompetence, learning stops.
crna_clinical_overlay: Misattributing bradycardia to “depth” when it’s OCR → improve diagnostic heuristics and triggers.

name: Violations
definition: Deliberate deviation from rules/procedures.
positive_example: Differentiates bad system design (procedures unusable) from willful risk.
negative_example: Normalization of deviance hides violations until harm occurs.
crna_clinical_overlay: Skipping timeout under pressure → culture + forced function + leadership reinforcement. ---

name: Swiss Cheese (Revisited for Classification)
definition: Harm occurs when multiple layers fail; distinguish latent conditions from active errors.
positive_example: Prevents over-focus on the last person in the chain.
negative_example: Used as explanation without remediation.
crna_clinical_overlay: Identify upstream causes (staffing, equipment, handoff gaps) plus point-of-care errors.

name: Just Culture
definition: Accountability is matched to behavior type: human error (console), at-risk behavior (coach), reckless behavior (discipline).
positive_example: Improves reporting and system learning.
negative_example: Mislabeling errors as “reckless” recreates blame culture.
crna_clinical_overlay: Promote near-miss reporting without punishment; enforce boundaries for truly reckless behaviors.

name: At-Risk Behavior
definition: Risk is taken without recognizing it (risk drift due to incentives, shortcuts, convenience).
positive_example: Coaching + environment redesign reduces recurrence.
negative_example: Calling it “bad attitude” misses the systemic driver.
crna_clinical_overlay: Shortcut sedation prep because “we always do it fast” → redesign setup and expectations.

name: Error-Producing Conditions
definition: Context factors increase error probability: time pressure, fatigue, noise, interruptions, poor layout.
positive_example: Shifts focus to fixable conditions.
negative_example: Using conditions as excuses avoids accountability.
crna_clinical_overlay: Identify and mitigate: interruptions during induction, missing supplies, inconsistent cart layout.

name: Error-Proofing Ladder
definition: Stronger controls: eliminate hazard → substitute → engineer controls → admin controls → training.
positive_example: Pushes toward durable fixes (design) over brittle fixes (training).
negative_example: Over-engineering can create workarounds.
crna_clinical_overlay: Prefer engineered label/layout solutions over “be more careful.” --- # Expansion Pack v12 — Team Communication Protocols

name: Closed-Loop Communication
definition: Sender states message → receiver repeats back → sender confirms/corrects.
positive_example: Prevents “heard but not understood.”
negative_example: Overuse on trivial matters slows flow.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use during meds, critical vitals changes, and airway events.

name: SBAR
definition: Situation → Background → Assessment → Recommendation.
positive_example: Faster, cleaner handoffs; fewer omissions.
negative_example: If used robotically, can omit nuance.
crna_clinical_overlay: PACU handoff: airway risk, meds, events, plan.

name: Callouts
definition: Loud, clear statements about critical information to the whole team.
positive_example: Aligns team attention quickly.
negative_example: Too frequent callouts create alarm fatigue.
crna_clinical_overlay: “Brady 38—possible OCR—stopping traction—treating now.”

name: Checkbacks
definition: Verification technique: restate information to confirm accuracy.
positive_example: Reduces misheard doses and instructions.
negative_example: Can feel patronizing if tone is wrong.
crna_clinical_overlay: “Confirm 10 mg ephedrine given?”

name: Two-Challenge Rule
definition: If a safety concern is ignored, assert twice; if still ignored, escalate to a higher authority/stop the line.
positive_example: Prevents silent failure when hierarchy blocks voice.
negative_example: If misused, can create interpersonal friction.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use when sterile cockpit is violated during induction or when incision proceeds without timeout.

name: CUS Words
definition: Standard escalation language: *Concerned* → *Uncomfortable* → *Safety issue*.
positive_example: Makes escalation explicit and harder to dismiss.
negative_example: If overused, can lose power.
crna_clinical_overlay: “I’m concerned about airway access once drapes are up. I’m uncomfortable proceeding without backup airway ready. This is a safety issue.”

name: Team Brief / Huddle / Debrief
definition: Brief = align plan; huddle = adjust; debrief = learn.
positive_example: Prevents surprises and improves learning.
negative_example: Perfunctory rituals without substance.
crna_clinical_overlay: 60-second morning brief; 30-second mid-day huddle if delays; 2-minute debrief on the biggest variance.

name: Speak-Up Culture (Psychological Safety)
definition: Teams perform better when members can raise concerns without punishment.
positive_example: Earlier detection of drift and hazards.
negative_example: “Safety theater” if leadership punishes dissent.
crna_clinical_overlay: Leaders model gratitude for concerns; separate reporting from blame. --- # CRNA / Clinical Systems Overlay — Errors + Communication (Quick Map) | Context | Models | Practical Use | |---|---|---| | Medication near-miss | Slips/Lapses; Error-Producing Conditions; Closed-Loop | Classify error, fix conditions, confirm dosing messages | | Missed checklist step | Lapses; External Cues; Standard Work | Add cue/checklist; log deviation; adjust workflow | | Misdiagnosed instability | Mistakes; Bayesian Updating; Callouts | Improve cues/heuristics; share critical info quickly | | Rule-breaking under pressure | Violations; Just Culture; Two-Challenge | Distinguish drift vs reckless; escalate appropriately | | PACU handoffs | SBAR; Checkbacks | Reduce omissions; confirm key risks and plans | --- # Expansion Pack v13 — OR Throughput + Queueing Deep Dive

name: Utilization (ρ) and the “Near-100% Trap”
definition: When utilization approaches 1.0, queues and delays grow nonlinearly; high variability makes it worse.
positive_example: Keeping a small capacity buffer prevents cascading delays and cancellations.
negative_example: Running “fully booked” without buffers guarantees overtime and late starts.
crna_clinical_overlay: If anesthesia coverage is scheduled at 95–100% with variable case times, expect frequent overflow into lunch/PACU bottlenecks.

name: Variability Buffering (Capacity, Time, Inventory)
definition: Variability must be absorbed by buffers: extra capacity, extra time, or extra WIP (patients waiting).
positive_example: Planned “slack” (time buffer) reduces unplanned overtime.
negative_example: Using WIP as the buffer (patients waiting) harms experience and safety.
crna_clinical_overlay: Prefer time/capacity buffers (staffing, PACU beds) over buffering with delayed patients.

name: Little’s Law (L = λW)
definition: Average WIP equals arrival rate times average time in system.
positive_example: Reducing PACU LOS reduces PACU census at the same arrival rate.
negative_example: Measuring only “speed” while ignoring arrivals creates blind spots.
crna_clinical_overlay: If cases keep arriving, the only sustainable way to lower PACU crowding is lowering LOS or increasing capacity.

name: Kingman’s Approximation (Variability Drives Waiting)
definition: Waiting time increases with utilization and variability in arrivals/service; variability is a first-class lever.
positive_example: Standardizing setup and reducing variability often beats “working faster.”
negative_example: Ignoring variability causes recurring “mystery delays.”
crna_clinical_overlay: Reduce variance in pre-op readiness and anesthesia setup to reduce downstream waiting more than shaving 1 minute off induction.

name: Bottlenecks and Blocking/Starving
definition: Bottlenecks limit throughput; upstream gets blocked (can’t send work) and downstream gets starved (no work) depending on constraint location.
positive_example: Fixing the constraint raises throughput system-wide.
negative_example: Optimizing non-bottlenecks increases WIP with no throughput gain.
crna_clinical_overlay: When PACU is full, rooms block; when pre-op isn’t ready, rooms starve. ---

name: WIP Limits (Pull Systems)
definition: Cap work-in-progress to prevent overload and stabilize flow; pull work only when capacity exists.
positive_example: A PACU “release valve” prevents flooding recovery.
negative_example: No WIP limits yields frantic surges and then stalls.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use a clear rule: do not bring the next patient back if PACU capacity is below threshold.

name: Batch Size vs One-Piece Flow
definition: Batching increases waits and variability; one-piece flow reduces time-in-system.
positive_example: Running patients individually through pre-op reduces bunching at induction.
negative_example: Big batch moves create synchronized congestion.
crna_clinical_overlay: Avoid “batching” consents/IVs that produce surges into the OR.

name: Setup Reduction (SMED)
definition: Reduce changeover time by separating internal vs external steps and standardizing.
positive_example: Prep meds/airway equipment outside the room to shorten turnover without rushing.
negative_example: Cutting turnover time by skipping safety steps increases risk.
crna_clinical_overlay: Define non-negotiable safety checks; move everything else “external” (prepped before room ready).

name: Takt Time vs Cycle Time
definition: Takt time = demand rate; cycle time = process rate. If cycle time > takt, backlog grows.
positive_example: Matching schedule demand to realistic cycle times reduces overtime.
negative_example: Overbooking hides mismatch until the day explodes.
crna_clinical_overlay: If surgeon pace and anesthesia cycle time can’t meet scheduled demand, the schedule—not the team—must change.

name: Standard Work (Best-Known Method)
definition: Define the safest, fastest repeatable process; reduce variability and enable improvement.
positive_example: Consistent MAC setup reduces errors and improves speed.
negative_example: Over-standardization can block necessary adaptation.
crna_clinical_overlay: Standard MAC setup: monitors → airway backup → meds ready → rescue thresholds posted.

name: Resource Pooling (Cross-Training)
definition: Pooling flexible resources reduces queueing compared to dedicated silos.
positive_example: Cross-trained staff can flex to pre-op, OR, PACU depending on the constraint.
negative_example: Over-pooling without role clarity causes diffusion of responsibility.
crna_clinical_overlay: Float roles assigned to the day’s constraint (pre-op readiness vs PACU discharges).

name: Priority Queues and Triage
definition: Not all work is equal; prioritize based on clinical urgency and system leverage.
positive_example: Fast-track short predictable cases to stabilize flow.
negative_example: Poor prioritization can feel unfair and damage trust.
crna_clinical_overlay: Use a transparent triage rule (e.g., time-sensitive add-on, then short predictable cases) to reduce chaos. ---

name: Leading vs Lagging Indicators
definition: Lagging metrics reflect outcomes; leading indicators predict them.
positive_example: “Pre-op readiness by T-20” predicts on-time starts better than end-of-day overtime.
negative_example: Measuring only lagging indicators delays correction.
crna_clinical_overlay: Track leading signals: patient in room by X, drape time, PACU bed availability, anesthesia ready stamp.

name: Balancing Measures
definition: Every speed metric needs safety/quality counter-metrics to prevent Goodhart failures.
positive_example: Turnover targets paired with airway interventions and PACU LOS prevent unsafe rushing.
negative_example: Single-metric optimization causes harm.
crna_clinical_overlay: Pair flow KPIs with rescue rate, hypotension episodes, nausea/vomiting, unplanned admissions.

name: Run Charts and Special Cause vs Common Cause
definition: Use time-series to distinguish normal variation from true process changes.
positive_example: Avoid whiplash reactions to one bad day.
negative_example: Missing real trend signals leads to chronic pain.
crna_clinical_overlay: Track weekly start times/turnover and identify special-cause events (staffing changes, new surgeon pattern). --- # Expansion Pack v14 — Decision Traps in Diagnosis & Clinical Safeguards

name: Anchoring
definition: Fixating on an initial impression and insufficiently adjusting as new data arrives.
positive_example: Speed in common patterns.
negative_example: Missed alternate causes when vitals evolve.
crna_clinical_overlay: Don’t anchor hypotension to “depth” if EtCO₂, HR, and field signals suggest obstruction, hemorrhage, OCR, or medication effect.

name: Premature Closure
definition: Stopping the diagnostic process once a plausible explanation is found.
positive_example: Efficient in low-stakes, high-confidence situations.
negative_example: Misses coexisting problems.
crna_clinical_overlay: After “airway obstruction fixed,” confirm ventilation, perfusion, depth, and equipment function before returning to baseline.

name: Confirmation Bias
definition: Seeking/interpreting evidence that supports the chosen hypothesis.
positive_example: Rapidly validates a correct hypothesis.
negative_example: Filters out disconfirming cues.
crna_clinical_overlay: Actively ask, “What would I see if I’m wrong?” and look for that sign.

name: Availability Heuristic
definition: Overweighting diagnoses that are recent, vivid, or emotionally salient.
positive_example: Recent learning can improve detection.
negative_example: Rare events become over-planned.
crna_clinical_overlay: A recent rare airway event shouldn’t convert every MAC plan into maximal sedation avoidance if patient/procedure doesn’t warrant it.

name: Representativeness
definition: Judging likelihood by pattern match, ignoring base rates and atypical presentations.
positive_example: Fast recognition of classic presentations.
negative_example: Misses atypical or mixed pictures.
crna_clinical_overlay: OCR may present atypically; treat brady patterns with traction cues even if not “classic.”

name: Diagnosis Momentum
definition: Once labeled, a diagnosis persists through handoffs and becomes sticky.
positive_example: Shared language speeds coordination.
negative_example: Wrong label persists and blocks reevaluation.
crna_clinical_overlay: In PACU handoff, distinguish facts from hypotheses: “Likely obstruction resolved” vs “confirmed obstruction.”

name: Overconfidence
definition: Confidence exceeds accuracy; reduces checking and second opinions.
positive_example: Decisiveness under time pressure.
negative_example: Missed checks; delayed rescue.
crna_clinical_overlay: Track your “easy MAC” calls vs rescue events to calibrate.

name: Outcome Bias
definition: Judging decision quality by outcome rather than process.
positive_example: Success can reinforce good habits.
negative_example: “It worked” can validate unsafe process.
crna_clinical_overlay: Review whether the plan was robust even when nothing bad happened.

name: Hindsight Bias
definition: After the fact, events seem predictable; learning gets distorted.
positive_example: Can surface missing cues.
negative_example: Unfair blame; false certainty.
crna_clinical_overlay: In debriefs, reconstruct the timeline and information available at the moment, not the outcome. ---

name: Diagnostic Timeout
definition: Brief pause to reassess: data → hypotheses → next test/intervention.
positive_example: Resets anchoring and premature closure.
negative_example: Poor timing can delay urgent action.
crna_clinical_overlay: After first rescue maneuver, do a 10–15 second timeout: “What changed? What didn’t?”

name: “Consider the Opposite”
definition: Deliberately search for evidence that would disconfirm your current hypothesis.
positive_example: Prevents confirmation lock-in.
negative_example: Overuse can slow action in obvious cases.
crna_clinical_overlay: If you think it’s depth, look for signs it’s not (ventilation change, traction timing, drug timing, cuff artifacts).

name: Differential Checklist (Minimum Set)
definition: A short forced list of common causes to check before finalizing.
positive_example: Prevents omitted common causes.
negative_example: Long checklists create fatigue.
crna_clinical_overlay: For hypotension: depth/vasodilation, hypoventilation/CO₂, OCR, hemorrhage, drug timing, monitor artifact.

name: Second Pair of Eyes
definition: Rapid consult or team query to reduce individual bias.
positive_example: Catches blind spots quickly.
negative_example: If culture punishes questions, it won’t happen.
crna_clinical_overlay: “I’m seeing X—what do you think?” during instability normalizes collaborative diagnostics.

name: Calibration via Post-Case Review
definition: Compare predictions vs reality to tune confidence and thresholds.
positive_example: Improves future diagnostic speed and accuracy.
negative_example: If reviews become blame sessions, learning collapses.
crna_clinical_overlay: Track: rescue events, causes, early signs missed, and the smallest earlier intervention that would have prevented escalation. --- # CRNA / Clinical Systems Overlay — Throughput + Diagnostic Debias (Quick Map) | Context | Models | Practical Use | |---|---|---| | Chronic late starts | Utilization; Variability Buffers; Leading Indicators | Add buffers, reduce readiness variability, track T-20 readiness | | PACU crowding | Little’s Law; Bottlenecks/Blocking | Reduce LOS or add capacity; prevent flooding with WIP limits | | Turnover variability | Kingman; Standard Work; SMED | Standardize, externalize steps, reduce variance more than mean | | Case-time overruns | Takt vs Cycle Time; Run Charts | Match schedule to reality; separate special vs common cause | | Intra-op instability misread | Anchoring; Premature Closure; Diagnostic Timeout | Force reassessment and a minimum differential checklist | | Sticky wrong handoff label | Diagnosis Momentum; SBAR + checkbacks | Separate facts vs hypotheses; confirm key risks |
